--- title: "Class imbalance" description: "When one answer is rare, a model can be highly accurate and still miss most of the rare cases. Logistic regression finds one presence of a rare species in six yet is 92% accurate, and rebalancing the training data turns out to do no more than move the threshold." order: 5 categories: [assumptions, class-imbalance, metrics] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Accuracy hides the misses when one answer is rare Some of the outcomes marine scientists most want to predict are rare: a protected species in a haul, a harmful algal bloom, a bleaching event. When one answer is much rarer than the other, the classes are **imbalanced**. [Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd#a-threshold-turns-a-probability-into-yes-or-no) gives each station a probability of presence, and a threshold turns it into a call of present or absent. A call can be wrong in two ways: a false alarm calls a station present where the species is absent, and a miss calls it absent where the species is present. Accuracy is the share of calls that are right. With a rare species, nearly every station is an absence, and calling an absence absent is easy. Accuracy mostly counts those easy calls, so it stays high even when the model misses most of the stations that matter. With a rare answer, count how many of the rare cases a model finds, not just how often it is right. [Classification performance measures](../07-validation/classification-metrics.qmd) names that share and the measures that go with it. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Rebalancing evens out the classes before fitting The common fix for imbalance is to change the data the model is fitted to, so that both answers are equally common. **Downsampling** drops cases of the common class at random until they match the rare one. **Upsampling** copies cases of the rare class at random until they match the common one. In R these are recipe steps from the `themis` package, so they change only the stations a model is fitted to. The stations it is scored on keep their real mix, as they must: upsampling the whole survey before splitting would put copies of the same station on both sides of the split, a kind of [information leakage](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd). ## Worked example The outcome is `rare_species`, a second species caught at only a few stations. The model is logistic regression on the six inputs, each entering as a straight line. The scores come from cross-validation by site, introduced in [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd). With so few presences, each of ten folds holds only a handful, so cross-validation is repeated five times with different folds, and every training station is predicted five times by models that never saw its site. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) folds <- group_vfold_cv(train, group = site_id, v = 10, repeats = 5) no_rebalancing <- recipe( rare_species ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season, data = train ) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> # dummies before rebalancing, so a fit that lacks a seabed type still runs step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) recipes <- list( "No rebalancing" = no_rebalancing, "Downsampling" = no_rebalancing |> step_downsample(rare_species), "Upsampling" = no_rebalancing |> step_upsample(rare_species) ) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train = survey.iloc[train_rows].reset_index(drop=True) folds = [fold for r in range(5) for fold in GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=r) .split(train, groups=train["site_id"])] numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical present = (train["rare_species"] == "yes").to_numpy() model = Pipeline([ ("recipe", ColumnTransformer([ # scaling leaves an unpenalised fit unchanged; it helps the solver converge ("numeric", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())]), numeric), # every level listed, so a fit that lacks a seabed type still runs ("categorical", OneHotEncoder( categories=[list(train[c].cat.categories) for c in categorical], drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical), ])), ("model", LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, max_iter=5000)), ]) # scikit-learn has no rebalancing step, so the fitting rows are resampled by hand def rebalance(rows, training, rng): yes, no = rows[present[rows]], rows[~present[rows]] if training == "Downsampling": no = rng.choice(no, size=len(yes), replace=False) if training == "Upsampling": yes = rng.choice(yes, size=len(no), replace=True) return np.concatenate([yes, no]) ``` ::: ::: The 598 training stations include only 29 with the rare species, 4.8% of them. ### Logistic regression finds one presence in six yet is 92% accurate Each recipe is fitted in every fold, and its predictions for the left-out sites are kept. `calls()` turns the predictions into calls at a threshold, as in [Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd), and gives three shares: of all stations, those called present; of the presences, those found; and of the absences, those called present, the false alarms. Applied at every threshold from 0 to 1 to the model fitted without rebalancing, it traces the model's whole range of answers. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predictions <- recipes |> imap(\(recipe, training) { workflow(recipe, logistic_reg()) |> fit_resamples(folds, control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |> collect_predictions() |> mutate(training = training) }) |> list_rbind() calls <- function(probability, truth, threshold) { yes <- probability >= threshold present <- truth == "yes" tibble(threshold, called = mean(yes), found = mean(yes[present]), false_alarms = mean(yes[!present]), accuracy = mean(yes == present)) } plain_predictions <- filter(predictions, training == "No rebalancing") by_threshold <- function(threshold) { calls(plain_predictions$.pred_yes, plain_predictions$rare_species, threshold) } curve <- map(seq(0, 1, by = 0.002), by_threshold) |> list_rbind() # the threshold that calls about as many stations present as hold the species matched <- curve |> slice_min(abs(called - prevalence), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) matched |> mutate(across(everything(), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| threshold| called| found| false_alarms| accuracy| |---------:|------:|-----:|------------:|--------:| | 0.194| 0.048| 0.166| 0.042| 0.919|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(123) pieces = [] for training in ["No rebalancing", "Downsampling", "Upsampling"]: for fitting, scoring in folds: kept = rebalance(fitting, training, rng) fitted = model.fit(train.loc[kept, predictors], present[kept]) pieces.append(pd.DataFrame({ "training": training, "present": present[scoring], "pred_yes": fitted.predict_proba( train.loc[scoring, predictors])[:, 1], })) predictions = pd.concat(pieces, ignore_index=True) def calls(probability, is_present, threshold): called = probability >= threshold return { "threshold": threshold, "called": called.mean(), "found": called[is_present].mean(), "false_alarms": called[~is_present].mean(), "accuracy": (called == is_present).mean(), } plain_predictions = predictions[predictions["training"] == "No rebalancing"] prevalence = present.mean() def by_threshold(threshold): return calls(plain_predictions["pred_yes"].to_numpy(), plain_predictions["present"].to_numpy(), threshold) curve = pd.DataFrame([by_threshold(t) for t in np.arange(0, 1.001, 0.002)]) # the threshold that calls about as many stations present as hold the species matched = curve.loc[[(curve["called"] - prevalence).abs().idxmin()]] matched.round(3).reset_index(drop=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | threshold | called | found | false_alarms | accuracy | |------------:|---------:|--------:|---------------:|-----------:| | 0.158 | 0.046 | 0.085 | 0.044 | 0.917 | ::: ::: ::: Logistic regression gives no station a probability much above 0.52, so the default threshold of 0.5 would call almost none present. Here the threshold is lowered to 0.19, where the model calls about as many stations present as hold the species. It finds about one presence in 6, and calls 4% of the absences present. Yet it is 92% accurate: reported as accuracy alone, a model that misses most of the presences would sound like a success. ### Upsampling gives the same answers as a lower threshold The rebalanced models are scored at the default threshold of 0.5, next to the model without rebalancing at a threshold equal to the share of training stations with the species. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} at_default <- predictions |> filter(training != "No rebalancing") |> summarise(calls(.pred_yes, rare_species, 0.5), .by = training) bind_rows(at_default, mutate(by_threshold(prevalence), training = "No rebalancing, threshold = prevalence")) |> mutate(across(threshold:accuracy, \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|training | threshold| called| found| false_alarms| accuracy| |:--------------------------------------|---------:|------:|-----:|------------:|--------:| |Downsampling | 0.500| 0.347| 0.676| 0.330| 0.670| |Upsampling | 0.500| 0.309| 0.717| 0.288| 0.712| |No rebalancing, threshold = prevalence | 0.048| 0.309| 0.717| 0.288| 0.712|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} at_default = pd.DataFrame([ {"training": training, **calls(group["pred_yes"].to_numpy(), group["present"].to_numpy(), 0.5)} for training, group in predictions.groupby("training", sort=False) if training != "No rebalancing" ]) pd.concat([at_default, pd.DataFrame([{"training": "No rebalancing, threshold = prevalence", **by_threshold(prevalence)}])], ignore_index=True).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | training | threshold | called | found | false_alarms | accuracy | |:---------------------------------------|------------:|---------:|--------:|---------------:|-----------:| | Downsampling | 0.5 | 0.424 | 0.615 | 0.415 | 0.587 | | Upsampling | 0.5 | 0.345 | 0.592 | 0.334 | 0.663 | | No rebalancing, threshold = prevalence | 0.045 | 0.341 | 0.569 | 0.33 | 0.665 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(curve, aes(false_alarms, found)) + geom_path(colour = "grey60", linewidth = 1) + geom_point(data = same, shape = 1, size = 6, stroke = 1.2) + geom_point(data = at_default, aes(colour = training), size = 3.6) + geom_point(data = matched, size = 3) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(Downsampling = ml_palette[["blue"]], Upsampling = ml_palette[["orange"]])) + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + labs(x = "Absences called present (false alarms)", y = "Presences found", colour = NULL, title = "Rebalancing moves along the threshold's curve, not above it", subtitle = paste("Grey: logistic regression without rebalancing,", "at every threshold")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The share of presences found against the share of absences called present, for logistic regression on the rare species, from cross-validation by site. The grey curve is the model fitted without rebalancing, at every threshold from 1 at the bottom left to 0 at the top right. The black point is that model at the threshold that calls about as many stations present as hold the species, and the open circle at a threshold equal to the share of stations with the species. The coloured points are the downsampled and upsampled models at the default threshold of 0.5.](class-imbalance_files/figure-html/fig-curve-1.png){#fig-curve fig-alt='A plot of the share of presences found, from 0 to 1, against the share of absences called present, from 0 to 1. A grey curve rises steeply from the bottom left corner and flattens towards the top right. A black point sits low on the curve, at 0.04 of absences called present and 0.17 of presences found. An orange point for upsampling sits on the curve at 0.29 and 0.72, over an open circle for the model without rebalancing at a threshold equal to the prevalence. A blue point for downsampling, at 0.33 and 0.68, sits below the curve.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: Upsampling at 0.5 and no rebalancing at a threshold of 0.048, the share of training stations with the species, give the same calls: both find 72% of the presences and call 29% of the absences present. Copying each presence about 20 times makes presence look about 20 times as common to the model, so it raises every station's probability but leaves the stations in the same order. Calling present above 0.5 after upsampling picks the same stations as calling present above about 0.05 without it. The rebalanced model now finds most presences, and its accuracy falls to 71%, because it calls many absences present. Lower accuracy, yet far more useful for finding the species: another reason not to judge a model on a rare answer by accuracy alone. Downsampling lands a little below the curve: at the same share of false alarms, a lower threshold on the model without rebalancing finds 75% of the presences where downsampling finds 68%. Each downsampled fit keeps only as many absences as there are presences, so it learns the absences from far fewer stations. ## A threshold set from the costs does the work of rebalancing Neither rebalancing nor a lower threshold makes the model better at telling presence from absence. Both choose where on the same curve to work, and the threshold does it without discarding stations. It also leaves the probabilities as they were: after upsampling, every station's probability is pushed up, so a probability of 0.6 no longer means a 60% chance of the species. Where to work depends on what each mistake costs. If a miss leaves a protected species unprotected, work far up the curve and accept the false alarms; if every station called present sends out a dive team, work lower down. [Choosing measures that match the objective](../07-validation/choosing-a-metric.qmd) turns the costs of the two mistakes into a threshold. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - With a rare answer, accuracy mostly counts the easy calls of the common answer. Logistic regression found one presence in 6 and was still 92% accurate. - Count how many of the rare cases a model finds, not just how often it is right. - Rebalancing, done in the recipe so that it changes only the stations a model is fitted to, moves a model along the curve the threshold traces: upsampling at 0.5 matched no rebalancing at a threshold of 0.048. - Leave the data alone and choose the threshold from the cost of each mistake. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. `step_downsample(rare_species, under_ratio = 3)` keeps three absences for each presence. Add it as a fourth recipe: where does its point land on @fig-curve? 2. Replace `logistic_reg()` with `rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("classification")`, as in [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd), and redraw @fig-curve. Does upsampling still land on the forest's own curve?
